utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-94-1-A, the Prosecutor versus Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Before the proceedings begin, I wish to apologise for the delay in calling the court to order. This was due to the unfortunate indisposition of a member of the Appeals Chamber, Judge Wang, who is unable to sit today. Technically, we are not properly constituted, I think, in his absence. I think that will be appreciated. So what we propose to do and to do only with your consent is this: We're waiting this afternoon on a procedural exercise to consider whether the sentencing phase should be remitted to a Trial Chamber and, if so, which Trial Chamber. What I propose, and again only with your consent, is that we hear the arguments, which I do not believe will be extensive, it being understood that these arguments will be considered by Judge Wang and that no decision will be taken without his full participation. In effect, when he rejoins the group, the matter will be reconsidered afresh by the Appeals Chamber in the light of any arguments you make which will be on the transcript. So the first thing is whether you would consent to that. If you do, then I should pass on to other matters. At the moment, technically, the bench is not properly constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, Your Honours, we have no objection to Your Honours proceeding with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure I speak on behalf of all counsel when we say that we hope Judge Wang is soon restored to full health. We have no objection to proceeding in his absence. It did occur to us that there may be provision for this in the rules as amended. Rule 15(E) as amended does deal with the question of the illness of a judge, and it there says that the President may authorise a Chamber to conduct routine matters in the absence of one or more of its members. We would have submitted that the proceedings today are only a routine matter in deciding the forum for the sentencing hearing, and if our reading of Rule 15(E) is correct, there may technically be a need for the authorisation of the President. But if that were forthcoming, then it's our submission that the four judges who are sitting today could proceed to make a decision in relation to the sentencing forum, and we would invite the Appeals Chamber to proceed, if it thinks that my reading of the rules is right, to make a decision today without Judge Wang's participation. If my reading of the rules does not find favour with the Court, then I would be content with the proposal that the Court has already made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution wish to make a contribution on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honours, our submission is that with regard to the argument to be presented, it could be presented before Your Honours as constituted at present, but on the question of the decision, I would submit that the absent judge should also take part in the decision making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Wang ought to take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Clegg, the bench appreciates your assistance. We had considered whether the hearing this afternoon could be comprehended by the reference to "routine matters". To say the least, we have doubts as to whether a decision as to whether this Chamber has competence or whether the competence resides with the Trial Chamber is, properly speaking, a routine matter. So what I propose is that we hear the arguments, as it were, ad referendum to Judge Wang and that he participates fully in the decision as to whether the sentencing should be done by this Chamber or should be done by a Trial Chamber. I'm very sorry. I appreciate the convenience of a certain point of view of going along the road which you had indicated, but it appears to us that there is no alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: So be it. One cannot let expediency override the rules of the Court, however tempting it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On that basis, the case has been called, and I take it that the appearances are as before. May I raise incidentally another matter? I don't think, Mr. Clegg, you are in the contempt case, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. That's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I have filed a motion in relation to that and was going to seek to be heard, but I would only advance that motion in the presence of Mr. Vujin because it seems to me that he would obviously have a right to be heard. Mr. Abell, I know, is in the building because I physically saw him arrive just before you sat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We would be glad if Mr. Abell could present himself for a limited purpose which is this, that we have the contempt case coming on. We have spoken with the President. It will be necessary in that case, we think, for a judge to be appointed to the place of Judge Wang, but that could only be done with the consent of the parties, we think. So we would need Mr. Abell in court -- really, we would need all the parties, but we can proceed with the participation of Mr. Abell on the basis that when the contempt case is called, we will represent the matter to all parties and hear their views. So if you are in a position to send for Mr. Abell, I would be grateful. Do I take it that the Prosecution agrees that in the contempt case, there could be a judge appointed to the place of Judge Wang?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: We do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, it was good of you to make yourself available to us. We have an unexpected conjuncture of circumstances this afternoon, and the resolution of those circumstances will affect the procedures relating to both the sentencing hearing and the contempt case. For reasons which may have already come to your notice, it appears to us that Judge Wang will not be able to participate in the contempt hearing. That means that the bench would not be properly constituted, unless we can have recourse to paragraph 5 of Rule 15 of the Rules which applied mutatis mutandis would enable the President to assign another judge to the case, but I think only with the consent of the parties. All the parties are not here, but you are here and the Prosecution is here, so we would like to know from you whether you would be agreeable to a replacement judge being appointed under that provision in relation to the contempt matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I would appreciate, before making any submissions on that, to have a brief opportunity to take instructions from Mr. Tadic, the interested party whom I represent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Indeed. I take it you would in turn appreciate that we would like to lay stress on the word "brief"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. May I say, I'm sorry to hear about His Honour, Judge Wang.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Indeed. Well, Mr. Abell, you will proceed. Meanwhile, we will return to the issue which brings us together this afternoon as to whether the Appeals Chamber is a proper Chamber for the purpose of sentencing or whether the matter should be remitted to a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, do forgive me for rising again, but in order to take instructions from Mr. Tadic, I will need briefly to retire with him in order to speak with him. That may require a short delay in the proceedings. I promise I will be brief, but I believe I have to speak with him about the matter first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you visualise that would involve an interruption in the proceedings relating to the sentencing matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Tadic is required for that. That's really a matter for my learned friend, Mr. Clegg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Clegg to indicate whether we may proceed in the absence of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I can see that Mr. Tadic is indicating that he would prefer to be present. If I could suggest that --

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I think I misinterpreted what Mr. Tadic -- we can proceed in the absence of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, you may retire with Mr. Tadic while we take up the sentencing proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I inquire as to whether Mr. Vujin is in the precincts? Has anybody any information?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: We've not seen him, but he's certainly been seen in the general area of the court but not inside the precincts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We can make a start with the arguments on the issue as to whether the Appeals Chamber has competence in relation to sentencing or whether that branch of the matter should be remitted to a Trial Chamber and, if so, which Trial Chamber. We issued a scheduling order last Friday in which we allocated 30 minutes to each side for this purpose, and I hope you find that adequate because you have already had an opportunity to submit written arguments, and we thought, looking at the character of the case, that it would be appropriate for the Prosecution, I think, to start and then for you, Mr. Clegg, to reply. Is that agreeable? Is that agreeable to the Prosecution as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes, it's agreeable to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution submits that a Trial Chamber composed of as many members of the original Trial Chamber as is possible is the most appropriate forum to deal at first instance with the question of sentencing on Counts 8, 9, 12, 15, 21, 29, 30, 31, and 32. There are two principal and related reasons for this submission. The first, Your Honours, is that the Tribunal Statute and Rules envisage that the Tribunal's discretion with respect to sentencing of a convicted person of any offence in the first instance is to be exercised by the Trial Chamber, and I would point to the submissions in our brief relating to Articles 23, 24, and Rule 101 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In comparison, there is no article in the Statute that refers to the authority of the Appeals Chamber to impose a sentence. In exercising its authority in this area, the Appeals Chamber is, in fact, bound by the provision of Article 25 of the Tribunal Statute which delineate the authority of the Appeals Chamber in considering judgements of a Trial Chamber on appeal. Article 25(ii) states that an Appeals Chamber may affirm, reverse or revise the decisions of a Trial Chamber. As interpreted by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, however, the authority granted in Article 25 also empowers the Appeals Chamber to determine and impose sentences. Rule 107, notably, states that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that are applicable to the Trial Chambers apply mutatis mutandis to the Appeals Chamber during the consideration of an appeal. That would include, of course, Rule 101 dealing with sentences. In addition, Rule 118(A) states that a sentence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- enforced immediately. Thus, while it is clear that the Appeals Chamber does possess the authority to impose sentences, the question raised is whether it is appropriate to exercise that authority in such cases as the present one, where the assessment of a new sentence arises solely from new or additional convictions based upon the reversal of a Trial Chamber's verdict by the Appeals Chamber. Under the Rules, there are at least three instances in which an Appeals Chamber may be called upon to impose a sentence, in our submission. The first instance is the one which the Appeals Chamber is now considering, whereas the result of an appeal of a judgement of a Trial Chamber, the Appeals Chamber has found the person guilty of new or additional charges. The second instance is where there has been an appeal on the sentence imposed by a Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber has found that the Trial Chamber committed an error of law or abused its discretion. The third instance is where the Appeals Chamber has found a person in contempt pursuant to Rule 77. The Prosecution submits it would be generally appropriate for the Appeals Chamber to determine and impose a sentence in both the second and third instances. When the Appeals Chamber has found someone in contempt, pursuant to Rule 77, the Appeals Chamber, as the finder of fact, would be the most appropriate body to impose the sentence since it would have direct knowledge of all the relevant factors. Similarly, where an appeal is brought alleging that a Trial Chamber abused its discretion in imposing a sentence, it might also be appropriate for the Appeals Chamber to impose a revised sentence if it determined that it had cognizance of all the relevant factors involved in the sentence. That may not be the case, however, where an appeal from a sentence is based upon a submission that the Trial Chamber wrongly excluded certain evidence or considered evidence that should have been excluded, and that determination, which calls for, in essence, a determination in the first instance of a new sentence, it might be more appropriate for the Appeals Chamber to return the case to the Trial Chamber for a reconsideration of sentence with instructions on the evidence to be considered. The Prosecution submits that it is these instances that Rule 118(A) was intended to apply. Where the Appeals Chamber pronounces new or additional findings of guilt, as it did in this case, it does so as a direct result of a revision of a verdict by a Trial Chamber. In this case, the decision to reverse the Trial Chamber's verdict was based solely upon an analysis of the Trial Chamber's legal reasoning and a determination by the Appeals Chamber that the Trial Chamber committed an error. It is significant that in reversing the Trial Chamber, the Appeals Chamber here did not question the underlying factual findings of the Trial Chamber or render any additional factual findings of its own. Rather, the reversal of the Trial Chamber was based solely on an analysis of issues of law. As a consequence, the imposition of a sentence based under these circumstances is not a mere revision after decision by the Trial Chamber, it is a de novo determination of a sentence. To undertake the determination of an appropriate sentence in the present case, the sentencing authority must consider all the relevant evidence and determine what aggravating and mitigating factors are present. That fact raises the issue of whether the interests of justice and the rights of the convicted person are not better served by having the trier of fact determine the appropriate sentence. The Trial Chamber was the trier of fact, with direct knowledge of the evidence in the case and direct observation of the witnesses and victims. Members of the Trial Chamber also have the benefit of their full reasoning and determination with respect to the case and the original sentence imposed. Conversely, should the Appeals Chamber determine that it will impose the sentence under these circumstances, it will, presumably, have to go back and review all the evidence related to the circumstances of the killings involved, for example, and the context in which they were committed. Moreover, the sentencing authority at the Tribunal does not enjoy the same advantages of courts that have authority to impose sentences in national jurisdictions. Those courts have the benefit of statutory provisions that establish the accepted range of punishments with particularity and, or in addition, they also have the benefit of a substantial amount of prior jurisprudence which provides clear guidance as to the appropriate sentences for various crimes. Due to the unique jurisdiction of the Tribunal, however, there is little in this manner to guide the Chambers in determining an appropriate sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you pause a minute to allow Mr. Tadic to return?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Consequently, due to the lack of prior jurisprudence and statutory provisions assisting the sentencing authorities at the Tribunal, there must be an even greater emphasis placed upon the particular circumstances in each case and an analysis of the factors set forth in Article 24(ii) and Rule 101. It is the Trial Chamber that is in the best position to give full effect to those issues, whereas the Appeals Chamber has had no opportunity to view the witnesses and victims or give consideration to the other factors. The second and related reason why it is more appropriate for the Trial Chamber to deal at first instance with the question of sentencing on these additional convictions is that this would afford the convicted person a possibility to appeal against the sentence on those counts. Consistent with Article 14 of the ICCPR, the Statute of the Tribunal, and within the unique jurisdiction and structure of this Tribunal, a right of appeal should be afforded at the appropriate junctures where the material rights of a party is affected by a decision. For these reasons, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that the appropriate course in this case is to remit the matter of sentencing to the original Trial Chamber if possible or, in the alternative, a Trial Chamber composed of as many members of the original Trial Chamber as is possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps this is an appropriate stage to ask Mr. Abell to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I thank you very much for the time you were kind enough to allow me to take instructions from the interested party, Dusko Tadic. The position is this: We do consent to the proceedings going ahead under the provision that Your Honour was kind enough to point out to me. May I say this, though? Under that particular section, it would appear that the person who has to consent is the accused, and Dusko Tadic is an interested party in the contempt proceedings. It would appear that the person whose consent is required is Milan Vujin, who is the accused for the purposes of these contempt proceedings. But, as I say, Mr. Tadic, if his consent is required, does consent and is willing for the matter to continue with a substitute judge. I take it that that substitute judge will have an opportunity to obviously consider the transcripts which have thus far been generated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, thank you very much. A substitute judge will have that opportunity, and you are quite right in saying that Mr. Vujin's consent will be necessary. I do not think you were present in the Chamber at an earlier stage when I said something to the effect that on the contempt case being called, we would have to return to the other interested parties. I think I said that. We didn't feel, like you, that we would be on safe ground in proceeding solely on the basis of your own consent. So we are ad idem on that. Thank you very much. In fact, our procedures this afternoon are somewhat unorthodox, as, indeed, is the constitution of the bench itself. We did put out a call for Mr. Vujin, seeking to discover whether he was available in the precincts. If he was, we would ask him now whether he also would consent. So your point has fully been taken on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, would it be convenient for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I confess for the second time in one afternoon, expediency and the desire for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, if you would like to retire at this point, we would be fully agreeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Of course. I had wondered whether I should actually remain. I will retire immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: My initial thoughts were reflected in paragraph 12 of the brief submitted on the 29th of July of this year which encouraged the Appeals Chamber to deal with the question of resentencing. That was before I had sight of the Prosecution brief and before I had the opportunity of hearing the submissions of Mr. Keegan. Since reading the brief of the Prosecution, I have reflected on the proper way to proceed, and I am satisfied that my original submissions were wrong and that the Prosecution's approach is, in fact, the correct approach. It was, I think, frankly a desire for expediency that persuaded me to urge the Appeals Chamber to determine the sentence for these offences that the appellant now stands convicted of for the first time, but for the second time today, I am forced to say that expediency is no substitute for proceeding in the proper way. I, frankly, am now convinced that the Prosecution's submissions are well-founded, and in those circumstances, we support them. My reasons are, firstly, that upon a proper analysis, we accept that the Statute and Rules clearly envisage that sentencing for offences should be done at the Trial Chamber level. Secondly, that preserves the appellant's right of appeal that would otherwise be lost, and I accept the submissions contained in paragraph 9 of the Prosecution's brief so far as that is concerned. Therefore, we find ourselves agreeing with the Prosecution and, like them, submit that the Trial Chamber which deals with the question of sentence should ideally be comprised of the same three judges that heard the trial itself. We are, of course, all conscious of the position of Judge Stephen. Recognising that difficulty, we would say that it is preferable that the remaining two judges of the original Trial Chamber should sit in the reconvened Trial Chamber for sentence, although that's not strictly essential under the Rules, but we would submit it's highly desirable that the other two judges do sit. I've reflected on what the Appeals Chamber should do in relation to the appeal against sentence that, of course, is pending in relation to the remaining counts. We would urge the Appeals Chamber to adjourn that appeal against sentence on the remaining counts until after the Trial Chamber sentences on the fresh offences, and we would then envisage the Appeals Chamber dealing with one consolidated appeal against sentence, embracing the sentence passed by the original Trial Chamber which is the subject of appeal, and if it's to be the subject of appeal, and one knows not what the Trial Chamber will do on the new convictions, but if that were to be the subject of a separate appeal, then we would anticipate this Appeals Chamber hearing a consolidated appeal dealing with all matters together. If the Appeals Chamber were attracted to that suggestion, then we would hope that the Trial Chamber could be convened for this very limited purpose within a very short time scale, and we would hope, at any rate, that the matter could be dealt with with reasonable expedition. Unless I can assist the Appeals Chamber any more, those are our submissions. The bad lawyer doesn't sometimes recognise that he's made a bad point, and I think, on reflection, our original position was erroneous, and we recognise that error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. The strength of a lawyer is the ability of the practitioner to revise his earlier thinking. So I do not think the bench would be disposed to find any fault with you for simply changing your opinion in the light of the opinion expressed by your colleagues on the other side. What I'd like to say to you, and for the record, is that this is a point which occurred to the bench. The bench has no position on it, but it considered that it would be wise to take counsel with both sides, and that is what we are doing today. The Prosecution has not had an opportunity to address the point which you made latterly to the effect, I think, that the decision on the sentencing appeal might be adjourned pending a determination by the Trial Chamber of the question of what sentences should be passed in relation to these counts on which the Appeals Chamber has held Mr. Tadic to be guilty but in respect of which he was acquitted earlier on. So perhaps I might invite the Prosecution to respond to that point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could, could we beg just a moment to confer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for your indulgence. It would be the submission of the Prosecution, Your Honours, that, in fact, it would be preferable to proceed with the appeal on sentencing as currently fashioned by the appellant, that within that appeal, there are a number of issues that may or may not be applicable to any resentencing on these distinct counts, but more particularly, it seems to us then the Trial Chamber would have the benefit of the guidance from the Appeals Chamber on the sentencing issues already raised in fashioning an appropriate sentence on these additional convictions, such that it may, in fact, avoid any potential error, assuming that the Appeals Chamber found that there was some in the first instance, with respect to these later counts, and, therefore, it would probably minimise to a great extent any potential issues for appeal. If there was a second appeal, it would only be limited -- it would be limited to just those discrete counts for which the additional sentence was imposed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So your submission, Mr. Keegan, is that if the Appeals Chamber were to remand the matter for sentences to be passed by a Trial Chamber, that that should not prevent the Appeals Chamber from now deciding on the sentencing appeal which has not yet been concluded. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then would that necessitate a modest revision of the position the Appeals Chamber took on 15 July? I think the Appeals Chamber then visualised that there would be a sentencing hearing on the counts on which Mr. Tadic was acquitted but which he has been found guilty by the Appeals Chamber, and that when sentences were passed on these counts, then at the same time, there would be a determination of the outstanding appeal relating to sentencing. On this format under which the matter would be remitted to a Trial Chamber, the Appeals Chamber would not be, in fact, sentencing anyone. So there would be a discrepancy there between the new position and the old position. Would we have to say that we are revising the decision of 15 July to mean this: that we would now determine the sentencing appeal at the same time at which a determination is made to remit the matter to a Trial Chamber? Is that a little too complex?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, if, in fact, the 15 July submission was based on the premise, which certainly we believed it was, that the Appeals Chamber would be imposing a sentence, then, yes, that would be correct; however, if, in fact, the position now is that the submissions on sentencing would be remitted back to a Trial Chamber, then, in fact, the situation is one of a clarification, and along the lines of our submissions with respect to the existing appeal on sentence, it would be the remission back to the Trial Chamber with instructions that a decision on the sentencing appeal as currently lodged would be following. In that situation, the Trial Chamber then has the benefit of the Appeals Chamber's guidance on the sentencing issues already raised at the time they decide on an appropriate sentence for the additional counts. That seems to us to affect the matter of efficiency and also perhaps solve potential difficulties for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, I wish to be clear. No doubt you were, but I didn't follow you exactly. You see, on the 15th of July, the Chamber said words to the effect that the outstanding sentencing appeal would be determined at the time when the Appeals Chamber would be imposing sentences in respect of the counts on which the Appeals Chamber has recorded convictions where there were previous acquittals. If the option were used of remitting sentencing to a Trial Chamber, that 15th of July decision would be inoperative. It would become difficult to apply. Would it then be necessary for the Appeals Chamber to revise that 15th of July decision to say that the sentencing appeal would now be determined at the same time when a decision is taken to remit the matter to the Trial Chamber in relation to the offences in respect of which the Appeals Chamber has now recorded convictions where there were acquittals previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The other option would be that the Appeals Chamber, in its order remitting the matter back, advises the Trial Chamber that it will decide the existing sentencing appeal as soon as possible or immediately so that the Trial Chamber has the benefit of that decision before it imposes additional sentences for the additional convictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then you're proposing a three-stage scenario like this: (1) The Appeals Chamber remits the matter to a Trial Chamber. (2) Thereafter, the Appeals Chamber decides on the outstanding appeal. (3) Thereafter, the Trial Chamber, in light of that intervening decision, then passes sentence. Is that the scenario you're painting for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Clegg, do you follow what your colleague is saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. I don't agree with it but I follow it. It seems to me that it's making very hard work of what I hoped would be a comparatively simple exercise. On the 15th of July -- I've just got the transcript in front of me -- what the Court said was that the appellant's appeal against sentencing judgement will be determined when a decision is made as to sentencing on those counts. So the Appeals Chamber clearly never envisaged the concept of deciding the appeal against the sentences that had been passed before anyone knew what the sentence was in relation to the other counts. It's a fundamental principle of the Appeals Chamber's function in determining an appeal against sentence, the concept of the totality of that sentence and whether the total sentence is right and proper, bearing in mind the offences for which the defendant or appellant has been convicted. Here, if the Appeals Chamber hears the sentencing on the counts that he has currently been sentenced on, the Appeals Chamber will effectively have to approach the appeal with blinkers and pretend he hasn't been convicted of the other offences at all because there's no sentence passed, and you can't consider, in deciding whether the current sentences were appropriate and the totality of that sentence was right, what may or may not be the sentence in relation to offences which he's never been sentenced for at all. Then you have the prospect of a further appeal on the other half, as it were. It's a piecemeal way of doing the -- of doing justice and, we would submit, an untidy way. There's a simple solution: It's remitted to the Trial Chamber. Hopefully it can be performed as speedily as possible. There will be a short sentencing hearing there, I can't imagine it would last more than an hour if briefs are filed by both sides, and then this Appeals Chamber can reconvene soon afterwards and hear the appeal as one consolidated appeal and decide the whole thing in the round. We would submit that has the attraction of implicitly, speed, and reduces the number of hearings by two, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What you're saying then is the 15th of July decision sensibly, if I may say, assumed the Appeals Chamber would be taking an integrated approach to the matter of sentencing and would be viewing the affair in its entirety, but that that block approach would now be fragmented if another solution were employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But not if your proposition were adopted, your proposal being that the decision on the sentencing appeal should be adjourned and resumed sometime after the Trial Chamber would have determined what are the sentences on the counts in question. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. Thank you. Mr. Keegan, you would like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just briefly. We believe that the 15 July decision was valid as an expeditious mechanism if, in fact, the Appeals Chamber, as you stated, was going to consider it. In this situation, if it is going to be remitted back to the Trial Chamber, it perhaps is not such an easy issue, and while simplicity is always preferable in language, it may not be so preferable in procedures of criminal law. We are a new jurisdiction. It would seem to us that the appeal here on sentencing would not have to be decided with blinkers. It would be decided on matters of law, the questions of law raised by the appellant. Those matters could be decided irrespective of the fact that the Trial Chamber still has to decide on additional sentencing. In fact, the benefit of such a decision would be to provide guidance to the Trial Chamber in its final analysis on additional sentencing. So while we appreciate that it may not appear at first glance to be the most efficient mechanism, it may, in fact, be the most preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, while you're on your legs, could you answer me one small question? Within your experience and learning, is there any precedent in any system of law for saying that a court is competent to convict but not competent to impose sentence in relation to that conviction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I am not aware of any system where that is the case, Your Honour, nor, in fact, is it our submission here. Our argument is not that the Appeals Chamber was not competent to impose sentence, the issue was whether it was the most appropriate course in this circumstance. And that is the substance of our argument, that it is more appropriate, given these circumstances, to allow the Trial Chamber to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, the word "appropriate" is quite useful but sometimes a little dangerous. You have to find that we have another kind of competence, that we have a competence to remit to a Trial Chamber that the convicting court has the competence to remit to another court to do the sentencing. Have you applied your mind to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, to the extent that we find that it falls within the inherent power of a Trial Chamber under Article 25, given the authority to the Appeals Chamber to reverse, revise a decision. It seems to fall within the inherent powers of an Appeals Chamber in all jurisdictions to then remand back to a finder of fact the case with the appropriate instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You refer to Rule 118(A).

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'd like the benefit of your interpretation of (B).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As indicated in our submissions, again it is clear from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that the Appeals Chamber has the authority to impose sentence, and we outlined what we thought were the three apparent situations in which an Appeals Chamber could impose sentence, including the present case, but it was our submission that in drafting the Rules or in looking at the spirit of the Rules, as a total document it appears to us that it was in the context of the two primary ways in which it would be appropriate for an Appeals Chamber to impose a sentence, that it was in those circumstances that Rule 118(A) was intended to apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that the word "judgement" in (B) includes sentence when read in the light of (A)?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It is not apparent from the face of it, Your Honour, for two reasons. One, it talks of either as having been acquitted on all charges or as a result of an order pursuant to Rule 65 which deals with provisional release. So, in fact, on its face it would appear that it is not speaking of a situation of sentence but is, in fact, only talking about those two particular cases, either acquittal or Rule 65 determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. I see. Thank you. You have looked at the Seventh Protocol to the European Convention on Human Rights --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I confess I don't have it with me, Your Honour. I'd have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- which accepts cases -- I think Article 2 accepts cases in which a conviction is recorded by a Court of Appeal in lieu of a previous acquittal by a first instance Court. You have not had occasion to address your mind to the implications of that provision?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I confess I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Mr. Clegg, is there anything you would need to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Only in answer to the question posed by the bench as to what other jurisdiction. As one finds the court that quashes an acquittal and replaces it with a conviction, remit for sentence, and one illustration is the Divisional Court of the Queen's Bench Division in England, referred to in the declaration by Judge Nieto-Navia in the judgement of this appeal, on page 147, at paragraph 4, where an acquittal by the Magistrate's Court is reversed by the Queen's Bench Division in England, then it will normally, if not invariably, remit to the Magistrate's Court for sentence. That is an illustration, I think, of what the court is seeking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, and that is very helpful indeed. Thank you very much. Well, may I consult with my colleagues for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, it remains for me to express the indebtedness of the bench, to counsel on both sides for the assistance they have rendered to the Court. The predicament in which the bench is faced is manifest to learned counsel. We propose this: That the proceedings would be made available to Judge Wang. We would discuss fully with him and a decision would be taken, and we would, by an appropriate notification, either reassemble the court for delivery of the judgement, or we would deliver the judgement in writing without any necessity to trouble the parties to come to court again. Is that an agreeable procedure, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It's certainly agreeable to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then we are through with the discussions on the issue on which the bench desired to have your assistance this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: at 3.20 p.m. sine die
